vision: Vigil is the trustworthy cockpit for autonomous agent work: nothing an agent claims is accepted without evidence, nothing destructive happens without a rail, and every run is fully replayable and auditable from disk. The road to v1.0 turns that promise from something that works on one engineer's laptop into something any operator can install, trust, and prove — where the evidence check inspects content rather than byte counts, the rails ship neutral, the budget guard actually stops the run, and the artifacts are safe to hand to an auditor.
north_star: An operator can hand Vigil a multi-phase validation plan, walk away, and afterwards prove — from artifacts alone, without trusting a single sentence the agent wrote — exactly what was done, what passed, what it cost, and what was blocked.

strategic_themes.name: Escape the author's machine
strategic_themes.description: DEFAULT_RAILS and the example config encode /Users/nick, the OmniRoute checkout, ports 20128/20219/20239 and a launchd label. Until defaults are neutral and there is a scaffold command, the tool has exactly one possible user.

strategic_themes.name: Make the trust claims literally true
strategic_themes.description: The product's differentiator is 'verdicts are evidence-checked, not trusted'. Today the check is existence plus non-zero bytes, so a truncated or wrong-content artifact still passes, and maxBudgetUsd is accepted but never enforced. Close the gap between the claim and the code.

strategic_themes.name: Survive the SDK and survive the author
strategic_themes.description: Unchecked `as unknown as {...}` casts against an exactly-pinned SDK, no CI, and a bus factor of one. Harden the boundary, test the integration, and make regressions fail before runtime.

strategic_themes.name: First-class non-TTY operation
strategic_themes.description: --plain exists but auto-denies approvals and emits prose. CI and SSH consumers need structured output, a machine-readable exit summary, and an approval channel that is not a TTY overlay.

strategic_themes.name: Runs as a managed corpus
strategic_themes.description: runs/ captures full tool inputs and outputs verbatim, is never pruned, and can contain secrets. Treat the run corpus as a first-class artifact: redacted, retained on policy, comparable, and exportable.

target_audience.primary: The author/operator — a solo engineer running high-risk, multi-phase deployment and migration work through a Claude Code agent, who needs hard proof that each step actually happened rather than agent prose claiming it did.
secondary: AI-assisted engineering leads auditing what an autonomous coding agent did on a production-adjacent machine
Platform/DevOps engineers running gated validation plans in CI or over SSH via --plain mode
Teams adopting the Claude Agent SDK who need observability, safety rails and cost visibility around agent runs
Reviewers/auditors who read run artifacts (events.jsonl, gates.json, cost.json) after the fact without the TUI
target_audience.user_sophistication: Expert. Assumes familiarity with Claude Code, the Agent SDK, terminal TUIs, JSONL log analysis and gated validation-plan authoring.
target_audience.adoption_blocker: A second user cannot install Vigil today without rewriting DEFAULT_RAILS and the example config to remove the author's personal paths, hosts and ports. Phase 1 exists to remove that blocker.

phases.name: Escape Velocity
phases.goal: A second engineer can install Vigil, run `vigil init`, and get a safe, neutral, honest run on their own machine — where a PASS means the evidence was actually inspected and a budget cap actually stops the run.
success_criteria: Zero occurrences of `/Users/nick`, `OmniRoute`, `.omp` or author-specific ports in shipped default configuration
A clean-machine install to first successful gated run takes under 10 minutes with no manual config editing
A gate whose Capture artifact exists but contains the wrong content is recorded as FAIL
A run that exceeds maxBudgetUsd halts and exits non-zero
phases.exit_gate: An external operator completes a full 3-phase validation plan run on a machine that has never seen the author's environment.

phases.name: Hardened Boundary
phases.goal: Regressions in SDK integration, rails or the TUI fail in CI rather than mid-run on a production-adjacent machine, and the SDK version can be upgraded without fear.
success_criteria: SDK messages are schema-validated at the boundary; malformed shapes raise a diagnostic RunEvent instead of throwing mid-run
The exact SDK pin is replaced by a supported range with a contract test suite proving compatibility
CI runs typecheck, tests and build on every push with coverage reported
End-to-end runner behaviour is tested against a stubbed SDK without network or a real Claude binary
phases.exit_gate: An SDK minor-version bump can be merged on green CI alone, with no manual smoke test.

phases.name: CI Native
phases.goal: Vigil is a first-class citizen in pipelines and over SSH: structured output for machines, an approval path without a TTY, and a run corpus that does not grow without bound.
success_criteria: `--json` emits a stable, versioned schema consumable by a CI step without parsing prose
A pipeline can gate a deploy on Vigil's exit summary alone
Approvals in non-TTY mode no longer silently auto-deny
Retention policy keeps runs/ bounded on a long-lived machine
phases.exit_gate: A GitHub Actions workflow gates a merge on a Vigil validation plan run end to end.

phases.name: Resume & Compare
phases.goal: Long multi-phase runs recover intelligently from failure, and the value locked in the run corpus is unlocked through comparison, diffing and shareable summaries.
success_criteria: A failed run resumes from the failing gate rather than restarting the plan
Evidence from a prior attempt is reconciled rather than silently trusted or silently discarded
Two runs of the same plan can be diffed on verdicts, evidence hashes and cost
phases.exit_gate: A 3-phase plan that fails at phase 2 is resumed to completion without re-executing phase 1.

phases.name: Open Platform
phases.goal: Vigil is publicly installable, extensible beyond the one plan format it understands, and no longer dependent on a single author's attention.
success_criteria: `npm i -g vigil` installs a working binary
A non-XML plan format can be gated through a user-supplied adapter
Rails and hooks can be supplied as user modules and linted before a run
Public API, changelog and release automation exist
phases.exit_gate: A contributor who is not the author ships a plan adapter without modifying core source.

features.title: Neutral default rails with environment profiles
features.description: Replace DEFAULT_RAILS' author-specific content with a portable, generic deny/warn set (destructive git operations, pattern kills, home-directory deletion, agent-instruction file edits) that contains no absolute user paths, hostnames or ports. Move the OmniRoute-specific rails (warn-real-omp-config, warn-live-db, no-checkout-main's Desktop/OmniRoute path) into a shipped example profile under profiles/, loadable via config. Introduce path-token interpolation (${HOME}, ${planRoot}, ${cwd}) so rails can express machine-relative intent portably.
features.rationale: This is the single hardest adoption blocker. Five of seven default rails reference the author's machine; one silently fails to protect anyone else's repo because it hardcodes a Desktop/OmniRoute path. Without this, every other feature is invisible to every other user.
source_pain_points: DEFAULT_RAILS and vigil.config.example.json encode the author's personal OmniRoute environment
Environment-specific defaults make the tool effectively unusable by anyone else without rewriting rails and config
acceptance_criteria: A grep for '/Users/nick', 'OmniRoute', '.omp', '20128', '20219', '20239' and 'launchctl' across src/ and shipped config returns zero matches

DEFAULT_RAILS protects against git stash, git checkout/switch outside a worktree, pkill -f/killall, rm -rf on any home directory, and edits to CLAUDE/AGENTS/GEMINI.md using patterns that contain no absolute user paths
Rail match strings support ${HOME}, ${planRoot} and ${cwd} interpolation, resolved at config load and unit-tested for each token
profiles/omniroute.json reproduces the previous author-specific rail behaviour and is loadable via config.profile or --profile
Existing tests in verdict-rails.test.ts pass unmodified against the neutral rail set, with added cases proving the checkout rail now fires for an arbitrary repo path
Loading an unknown profile name fails config validation with a named error listing available profiles

user_stories.as_a: engineer installing Vigil for the first time
user_stories.i_want: default safety rails that protect my repository rather than someone else's
user_stories.so_that: I get real blast-radius protection without reading and rewriting the rail source

user_stories.as_a: operator with a specific production environment
user_stories.i_want: to layer an environment profile of extra rails on top of the neutral defaults
user_stories.so_that: I can encode my own live databases and config files as warn/deny targets without forking the tool

features.title: `vigil init` config and plan scaffolding
features.description: An interactive and --yes-scriptable init command that detects the environment (Claude Code binary location, git root, whether a worktree is in use), writes a validated vigil.config.json with sensible neutral defaults, optionally scaffolds a phases/ skeleton with an example PLAN.md and ROADMAP.md, and prints the resolved configuration including which rails are active and where runs will be written.
features.rationale: Discovery shows install is `npm link` from a Desktop checkout with no documented path from zero to a first run. Pairing a neutral rail set with a scaffold turns a two-hour archaeology session into a single command.
source_pain_points: README install instructions target ~/Desktop/vigil and npm link for personal PATH use
No published npm package — install is npm link from a Desktop checkout
acceptance_criteria: `vigil init` in an empty directory writes a vigil.config.json that passes ConfigSchema.parse without edits
`vigil init --yes` runs non-interactively with zero prompts and is safe to invoke in a script
Init resolves and reports the Claude Code executable using the existing --claude-bin → CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH → which claude → SDK default chain, and warns clearly if none is found
`vigil init --with-plans` scaffolds phases/01-example/01-01-PLAN.md plus ROADMAP.md that parse cleanly through the existing plan parser and produce at least one validation gate
Init refuses to overwrite an existing vigil.config.json unless --force is passed
Post-init output lists active rail ids, the resolved runs/ directory, the model, and whether settingSources is empty (clean agent)

user_stories.i_want: one command that produces a working configuration
user_stories.so_that: I can run my first gated plan without reverse-engineering the Zod schema

user_stories.i_want: a scaffolded example plan that already satisfies the runner contract
user_stories.so_that: I learn the Capture and verdict-line format by example rather than by failed runs

features.title: Content-aware evidence assertions with hash recording
features.description: Extend Capture targets from existence-plus-non-zero-bytes to declarative content assertions: minimum byte size, regex match, JSON-path existence or value comparison, and expected line count. Record a SHA-256 hash and byte size of every verified artifact into gates.json. A PASS whose assertion fails is downgraded to FAIL with the specific failing assertion injected back into the live session, reusing the existing evidence-downgrade path.
features.rationale: The product's core differentiator is that verdicts are evidence-checked rather than trusted, but the check is currently satisfied by any non-empty file. An agent that writes one byte of garbage to the Capture path passes the gate — the exact failure mode Vigil exists to prevent. Hashes also unlock run comparison in Phase 4.
source_pain_points: Evidence verification is existence + non-zero bytes only — a truncated or wrong-content artifact still passes
Validation reports written by the agent are self-graded
Agent prose is unverifiable: PASS claims are not backed by artifacts on disk
acceptance_criteria: The plan parser accepts assertion syntax on Capture lines covering at minimum: minBytes, matches (regex), jsonPath, and equals/contains for the resolved value
A Capture target with no assertion retains today's existence + non-zero-bytes semantics, so all existing fixture plans pass unchanged
A gate claiming PASS whose artifact exists but fails its regex assertion is recorded as FAIL in gates.json with a reason naming the assertion and the artifact path
The failing-assertion instruction is injected into the live session via the existing inject path and appears in events.jsonl
GateRecord.evidence entries gain sha256 and bytes fields, populated for every verified artifact including glob/brace expansions
Assertion evaluation is bounded: files above a configurable maxAssertBytes are streamed or rejected rather than read wholly into memory
Unit tests cover each assertion type passing and failing, plus malformed assertion syntax producing a parse-time error rather than a silent skip

user_stories.as_a: operator running a deployment validation plan
user_stories.i_want: gates to verify that evidence files contain what they should, not merely that they exist
user_stories.so_that: an agent cannot satisfy a gate by touching an empty or garbage file

user_stories.as_a: auditor reading gates.json after the fact
user_stories.i_want: a cryptographic hash of every artifact that backed a PASS
user_stories.so_that: I can prove the evidence on disk today is the evidence the gate actually accepted

features.title: Enforced budget and turn guards
features.description: Implement Vigil-side enforcement of maxBudgetUsd and maxTurns: track cumulative cost across plans in a run, emit a budget.warn RunEvent at configurable thresholds (default 75% and 90%), and hard-stop the run at 100% by interrupting the turn, writing a terminal budget.exceeded event and exiting non-zero. Surface remaining budget as a live header element in the cockpit and in --plain output.
features.rationale: maxBudgetUsd is accepted in config and handed to the SDK but never enforced locally, and cost is reported by the SDK rather than independently guarded. For a tool whose premise is walking away from an autonomous run, an unenforced spend cap is a direct financial risk.
source_pain_points: maxBudgetUsd is accepted in config and passed to the SDK, but there is no Vigil-side budget guard, warning or hard stop
Cost accounting is reported by the SDK, not independently verified; maxBudgetUsd is unenforced locally
acceptance_criteria: Cumulative run cost is accumulated from session.result events across all plans and persisted to cost.json as a run-level total
Crossing a warn threshold emits a budget.warn RunEvent exactly once per threshold and renders visibly in both the TUI header and --plain output
Reaching maxBudgetUsd interrupts the active turn, halts plan sequencing, writes a budget.exceeded event and exits with a distinct non-zero code
maxTurns is enforced with the same warn-then-stop semantics
When no maxBudgetUsd is configured, behaviour is unchanged and no budget events are emitted
A unit test drives synthetic session.result events past the cap and asserts the run halts before the next plan starts
The cockpit header shows spend against cap as an absolute and percentage value when a cap is set

user_stories.as_a: operator starting a long autonomous run and walking away
user_stories.i_want: a spend cap that actually stops the run
user_stories.so_that: a runaway loop cannot cost me hundreds of dollars overnight

user_stories.i_want: to see remaining budget live
user_stories.so_that: I can intervene before a cap forces an abrupt halt mid-phase

features.title: Secret redaction in run artifacts
features.description: Redact secrets before they reach disk. Apply a configurable redaction pass to tool inputs/outputs and event payloads covering known token shapes (ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and the configured authTokenEnv value, sk- prefixed keys, bearer headers, AWS keys, private key blocks, .env assignments) plus user-supplied redact patterns. Replace matches with a stable placeholder that preserves a hash prefix so distinct secrets remain distinguishable in an audit without being recoverable.
features.rationale: Tool artifacts store full inputs and outputs verbatim, and runs/ is never pruned. Every run that reads a .env or echoes a header writes a live credential to disk permanently — an audit trail that is itself a liability, which blocks sharing run artifacts with the auditors the product targets.
source_pain_points: Tool artifacts store full inputs and outputs verbatim: runs/ can contain secrets
Auth token read from an env var or plaintext config field — no keychain/secret-manager integration
acceptance_criteria: Redaction is applied in RunStore.append before any write, so events.jsonl, tools/*.txt, gates.json and cost.json are all covered by a single chokepoint
The resolved auth token value is redacted by exact match regardless of pattern coverage
Built-in patterns detect sk-* keys, Authorization/Bearer headers, AWS access key ids and secrets, PEM private key blocks, and KEY=value assignments for names matching /TOKEN|SECRET|PASSWORD|KEY/
config.redact accepts additional user regex patterns, validated at config load with a clear error on an invalid pattern
Redacted values render as [redacted:<8-char-hash>] so two different secrets remain distinguishable across a run
Redaction throughput is benchmarked and adds under 10% overhead on a synthetic 10k-event run
A test writes a fixture tool output containing each supported secret shape and asserts no raw secret survives to disk

user_stories.as_a: operator whose agent reads .env files during a run
user_stories.i_want: credentials scrubbed from run artifacts automatically
user_stories.so_that: my audit trail is not a permanent plaintext secret store

user_stories.as_a: engineering lead reviewing an agent run
user_stories.i_want: to share a runs/ directory with a colleague or auditor
user_stories.so_that: the evidence can be reviewed without leaking production credentials

features.title: Schema-validated SDK message boundary
features.description: Replace the unchecked `as unknown as {...}` casts in session.ts with Zod schemas for every consumed SDK message shape (assistant/result/system messages, hook payloads, canUseTool requests, usage and rate-limit structures). Validation failures emit a diagnostic RunEvent naming the offending shape and degrade gracefully rather than throwing mid-run. Widen the exact SDK pin to a supported semver range once the boundary is proven by contract tests.
features.rationale: Discovery names SDK coupling via unchecked casts with a pinned exact version as a top risk. The pin blocks upgrades; the casts mean an SDK schema change surfaces as a runtime crash in the middle of a production-adjacent run rather than as a test failure.
source_pain_points: Hard dependency on the Claude Agent SDK's message shapes; many handlers cast through `as unknown as {...}` and will break on SDK schema changes
SDK version is pinned exactly, which blocks upgrades
No CI, so regressions in the TUI or SDK integration surface only at runtime
acceptance_criteria: Every SDK message shape consumed by session.ts has a named Zod schema in a dedicated boundary module
A grep for 'as unknown as' in src/engine/session.ts returns zero matches
An unrecognised or malformed SDK message emits a diagnostic RunEvent at warn level and the run continues, rather than throwing
Recorded SDK message fixtures are captured from a real run and replayed through the boundary in a contract test suite
package.json declares a semver range for @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk rather than an exact pin
The contract suite passes against both the current pinned version and the latest release in the declared range
Verdict detection, cost parsing, rate-limit handling and hook decisions each retain dedicated tests proving behaviour is unchanged after the refactor

user_stories.as_a: operator mid-run on a production-adjacent machine
user_stories.i_want: an unexpected SDK message to be logged rather than crash the runner
user_stories.so_that: a library change never destroys an in-flight multi-phase validation

user_stories.i_want: contract tests against recorded SDK fixtures
user_stories.so_that: I can upgrade the SDK on the strength of green CI instead of a manual smoke test

features.title: CI pipeline with coverage reporting
features.description: A GitHub Actions workflow running typecheck, vitest with coverage, and build on every push and pull request across Node 20 and 22. Coverage is reported per run with a floor that fails the build on regression, starting at the current measured baseline and ratcheting upward.
features.rationale: There is no CI configuration and two commits of history. Every subsequent hardening feature in this roadmap is worth less without an automated gate that proves it stays true.
source_pain_points: No CI configuration, no release automation, no changelog
No coverage reporting
Solo author, 2 commits of history — bus factor of one
acceptance_criteria: A workflow at .github/workflows/ci.yml triggers on push and pull_request
The job matrix covers Node 20 and Node 22 and runs npm run typecheck, npm run test and npm run build
Vitest is configured with v8 coverage and a `test:coverage` script
A coverage floor is enforced and set to the measured baseline at implementation time; dropping below it fails the build
The workflow completes in under 5 minutes on a cold cache
A deliberately introduced type error and a deliberately failing test each cause a red build, verified once before merge

user_stories.i_want: typecheck, tests and build to run automatically on every push
user_stories.so_that: regressions surface before they reach a real agent run

user_stories.i_want: a visible passing build
user_stories.so_that: I can trust the project is maintained and my change did not break it

features.title: End-to-end runner harness against a stubbed SDK
features.description: A test harness that injects a scripted fake Agent SDK into the runner, driving full plan sequencing without network access or a Claude Code binary. Scenarios cover: a clean multi-plan pass, a FAIL halting sequencing, an evidence-downgrade with re-injection, a rail deny surfacing to the agent, the nudge-once path on a missing plan verdict, and budget exhaustion. Each scenario asserts on the resulting on-disk artifacts, exercising RunStore for the first time.
features.rationale: Discovery lists no end-to-end runner test and no store/artifact tests as explicit gaps. The riskiest orchestration logic — sequencing, halting, downgrade and re-injection — is precisely the logic with no automated coverage, and it is the logic that encodes the product's trust guarantees.
source_pain_points: No end-to-end runner test against a stubbed SDK
No store/artifact tests
No probes tests
No config/env-building tests
acceptance_criteria: The SDK dependency is injectable into PlanSession so tests supply a scripted message stream with no network or binary required
An e2e test runs the existing omp-live-deploy fixture end to end and asserts events.jsonl, gates.json, cost.json and tools/*.txt contents
A scenario proves a FAIL verdict halts sequencing and leaves subsequent plans unstarted
A scenario proves a PASS with missing evidence is downgraded to FAIL and an instruction is injected
A scenario proves a rail deny blocks the tool call and surfaces the deny reason to the agent
A scenario proves budget exhaustion halts the run, integrating with VG-004
RunStore, probes and config env-building each gain direct unit tests, closing the named coverage gaps
The full e2e suite runs in under 30 seconds in CI

user_stories.i_want: end-to-end coverage of sequencing, halting and downgrade behaviour
user_stories.so_that: I can change the orchestration without silently breaking the trust guarantees

user_stories.i_want: automated proof that on-disk artifacts match what the runner observed
user_stories.so_that: I can rely on runs/ as the source of truth rather than the TUI

features.title: Rail evaluation hardening against shell indirection
features.description: Improve rail matching beyond a single regex over a flattened string. Normalise the command before evaluation: strip quoting, expand simple variable assignments defined in the same command, decode inline base64 passed to eval or sh, split on shell operators and evaluate each segment independently. Add an optional strict mode that denies commands using known obfuscation constructs outright, and report per-rail false-positive risk through a new `vigil rails explain` subcommand.
features.rationale: Discovery states rails are bypassable via shell indirection and prone to false positives, while approvals auto/gates run with bypassPermissions — making rails the only gate on tool execution in the default mode. A trivially bypassable sole gate is the most dangerous kind of safety theatre.
source_pain_points: Rails are regex over a flattened tool-input string: bypassable via shell indirection (variables, base64, aliases) and prone to false positives
approvals auto/gates run with bypassPermissions — rails are the only gate on tool execution in the default mode
acceptance_criteria: Commands are split on ;, &&, ||, | and newlines, with each segment evaluated against every rail independently
Single and double quoting is stripped before matching so 'git' 'stash' and git""stash are both caught
Variable assignments within the same command are substituted before evaluation (e.g. C='git stash'; $C is denied)
base64 payloads piped to sh, bash or eval are decoded once and evaluated, with depth limited to prevent pathological input
config.railsStrict denies any command containing eval, base64 -d piped to a shell, or a here-doc executed as a script
`vigil rails explain '<command>'` prints which rails match, which segments triggered them, and the resulting action without executing anything
A dedicated bypass test suite covers at minimum 12 known indirection techniques and asserts each is caught
A false-positive suite asserts benign commands mentioning rail keywords in comments or filenames are not denied

user_stories.as_a: operator relying on rails as the only gate in auto mode
user_stories.i_want: rails that survive obvious shell obfuscation
user_stories.so_that: a destructive command cannot slip through by being assigned to a variable first

user_stories.i_want: to test a command against my rails without running anything
user_stories.so_that: I can tune patterns before trusting them in a live run

features.title: TUI snapshot tests for panes and overlays
features.description: Snapshot-render every pane and overlay through ink-testing-library against fixture UIState values produced by the existing reducer. Cover the wide and stacked (sub-110-column) layouts, every overlay (evidence, tool detail, approval, gate approval, inject, halt), and truncation behaviour at narrow widths.
features.rationale: Discovery names no Ink/TUI rendering tests as a gap while noting the layout stacks and heavily truncates below 110 columns. The cockpit is the primary interface and currently the least tested surface.
acceptance_criteria: ink-testing-library is wired into the vitest setup and renders without a TTY in CI
Every pane (header, plan/gate, transcript, tools, diagnostics) has a snapshot at both wide and stacked widths
Every overlay has at least one snapshot covering its populated state
Snapshots are driven by UIState built through the real reducer from fixture RunEvents, not hand-constructed state
A truncation test asserts no pane emits lines wider than the configured terminal width at 80, 110 and 160 columns
The global process.stderr.write monkey-patch is asserted to be installed on mount and fully restored on unmount
TUI tests run in CI in under 15 seconds

user_stories.i_want: snapshot tests across terminal widths
user_stories.so_that: I discover broken truncation in CI rather than mid-run at 80 columns over SSH

features.title: LICENSE, CONTRIBUTING and public API documentation
features.description: Add an OSI license file, a CONTRIBUTING guide covering local setup and the test strategy, and reference documentation for the config schema, plan format, runner contract, RunEvent union and the on-disk artifact layout that external consumers parse.
features.rationale: Discovery notes no license file, no CONTRIBUTING and no documented public API in-repo. The absence of a license legally blocks any adoption by the secondary audiences the product targets, and undocumented artifact schemas make the auditor persona impossible to serve.
acceptance_criteria: An OSI-approved LICENSE file exists and package.json declares a matching license field
CONTRIBUTING.md documents local setup, running tests, the layering rules and the expectation that pure logic is unit-tested
docs/plan-format.md specifies the XML-ish block grammar, Capture syntax including assertions, and the runner contract verdict lines
docs/artifacts.md specifies the schema of events.jsonl, gates.json, cost.json and session.json for external consumers
docs/config.md is generated from or verified against ConfigSchema so it cannot drift silently
The README links to all of the above and no longer hardcodes ~/Desktop/vigil as the install path

user_stories.as_a: engineering lead evaluating Vigil for my team
user_stories.i_want: a clear license
user_stories.so_that: I can get approval to use it on company machines

user_stories.as_a: auditor building tooling over run artifacts
user_stories.i_want: documented artifact schemas
user_stories.so_that: I can parse events.jsonl without reading the TypeScript source

features.title: Report generation for mid-phase and partial runs
features.description: Decouple report generation from the presence of a phase gate. Emit a VALIDATION.md for any plan that produced gate records, mark incomplete runs explicitly as partial, and resolve the pending-gate gap so gates left unrun after a failure are recorded as 'not run' rather than silently pending. Replace the 30-second verdict de-duplication heuristic with idempotency keyed on gate id plus verdict plus evidence hash.
features.rationale: Discovery flags three related correctness gaps: reports only fire for plans containing a phase gate so mid-phase runs produce no report, pending gates after a failure are left in an explicitly empty branch, and the de-dup time window could suppress a legitimate rapid re-verdict. Together they mean the generated report — the product's audit deliverable — can be missing or wrong.
source_pain_points: Reports only fire for plans containing a phase gate (or on failure), so mid-phase runs produce no report
Pending gates after a failure are explicitly left pending (empty branch in runner.runOne)
Verdict de-duplication uses a 30s time window heuristic that could suppress a legitimate rapid re-verdict
acceptance_criteria: Any plan producing at least one gate record generates a VALIDATION.md, regardless of whether it contains a phase gate
Reports for incomplete runs carry an explicit 'PARTIAL' status marker in both the header and the ROADMAP.md status row
Gates never reached because a prior gate failed are recorded with a distinct 'not_run' verdict, not left pending
Verdict de-duplication is keyed on gateId + verdict + evidence hash rather than a 30-second window
A test proves two legitimate distinct verdicts for the same gate within one second are both recorded
A test proves a byte-identical duplicate verdict line is recorded once
Existing reports.test.ts assertions continue to pass

user_stories.as_a: operator running a single mid-phase plan
user_stories.i_want: a validation report for that run
user_stories.so_that: partial work is still auditable without completing an entire phase

user_stories.i_want: unreached gates distinguished from failed gates
user_stories.so_that: I can tell what was never attempted from what was attempted and rejected

features.title: Structured JSON output and machine-readable exit summary
features.description: A `--json` mode emitting newline-delimited RunEvents on stdout under a versioned envelope, plus a terminal summary object containing per-plan and per-gate verdicts, evidence paths with hashes, total cost, blocked rail hits and a stable exit code taxonomy. Diagnostics are routed to stderr so stdout stays machine-parseable.
features.rationale: Discovery calls for structured JSON output for CI consumption and a machine-readable exit summary. Today --plain emits timestamped prose, so a pipeline must regex agent output to learn whether a gate passed — reintroducing exactly the unverifiable-prose problem Vigil exists to eliminate.
source_pain_points: Non-TTY parity: structured JSON output for CI consumption and a machine-readable exit summary
Post-hoc auditing requires reconstructing what happened from scrollback that is already gone
acceptance_criteria: `vigil run --json` emits one JSON object per line on stdout and nothing else; all human diagnostics go to stderr
Each emitted line carries a schemaVersion field and validates against a published JSON Schema
A final summary object reports per-plan verdicts, per-gate verdicts with evidence paths and hashes, total cost, turns and all rail hits
Exit codes follow a documented taxonomy distinguishing success, gate failure, budget exceeded, rail deny halt, and internal error
`--json` implies non-interactive operation and is accepted alongside prompt, run and replay commands
Piping stdout to jq in a CI example succeeds without preprocessing, proven by a test
The JSON Schema is committed and a test validates emitted output against it

user_stories.i_want: a machine-readable verdict summary and a meaningful exit code
user_stories.so_that: my pipeline can branch on the result without parsing prose

user_stories.i_want: a stable versioned event schema on stdout
user_stories.so_that: I can stream Vigil runs into our observability stack

features.title: Non-TTY approval channel
features.description: Give plain and JSON modes a real approval path instead of auto-denying. Support a pre-declared policy file of allow/deny rules evaluated per tool call, an optional FIFO/socket channel through which an external supervisor can answer approval requests with a configurable timeout, and a documented default-on-timeout behaviour per approval mode.
features.rationale: Discovery notes plain mode auto-denies tool approvals rather than offering a non-TTY approval channel, which makes the gates and all approval modes unusable in CI or over SSH — the exact contexts --plain was built for.
source_pain_points: Plain mode auto-denies tool approvals rather than offering a non-TTY approval channel
acceptance_criteria: A policy file declares allow/deny rules by tool name and pattern, evaluated before any interactive prompt
An approval request unmatched by policy is emitted as a JSON event and awaits a response on the configured channel
config.approvalTimeoutSec bounds the wait, with per-mode default-on-timeout behaviour documented and tested
A supervisor script in the test suite answers approvals over the channel and drives a run to completion
Gate approvals in `gates` mode work through the same channel as tool approvals
When no channel is configured, behaviour falls back to today's auto-deny with an explicit warning naming the denied tool
Approval decisions and their source (policy, channel, timeout) are recorded in events.jsonl

user_stories.as_a: DevOps engineer running gated plans in CI

user_stories.i_want: to answer approval prompts from a separate process

features.title: Run retention and pruning policy
features.description: Configurable retention over the run corpus by age, count and total size, applied via an explicit `vigil prune` command and an optional automatic sweep at run start. Failed runs and runs pinned by the operator are protected by default. A dry-run mode reports exactly what would be removed and how much space is reclaimed.
features.rationale: Discovery states runs/ is written under the plan root and is never pruned, while tool artifacts store full inputs and outputs verbatim. On a long-lived operator machine this grows without bound, and unbounded retention compounds the secret-exposure risk addressed in VG-005.
source_pain_points: runs/ is written under the plan root (or <cwd>/.vigil/runs) and is never pruned
runs/ can grow large with no rotation or retention policy
acceptance_criteria: config.retention supports maxAgeDays, maxRuns and maxTotalBytes, any subset of which may be set
`vigil prune <planRoot>` applies the policy and reports each removed run with reclaimed bytes
`vigil prune --dry-run` makes no filesystem changes and reports the same plan of action
Runs whose final verdict was FAIL are retained by default unless --include-failed is passed
`vigil runs --pin <id>` marks a run as never-prune and pruning respects the marker
Automatic pruning at run start is opt-in via config.retention.auto and never removes the current run
A test builds a synthetic corpus exceeding every limit and asserts the correct runs survive

user_stories.as_a: operator running Vigil daily for months
user_stories.i_want: old runs pruned automatically on a policy
user_stories.so_that: my disk does not fill with verbatim tool output

user_stories.i_want: failed and pinned runs retained by default
user_stories.so_that: cleanup never destroys the evidence I most need

features.title: Aggregate cost reporting across runs
features.description: A `vigil cost` command aggregating spend across the run corpus with grouping by plan, phase, model and time window, cache-token split, and output in table or JSON form. Includes per-gate cost attribution so operators can see which validation gates are expensive to satisfy.
features.rationale: Per-run cost.json already exists but nothing aggregates it. Discovery lists aggregate cost reporting across runs as an opportunity, and it is the natural companion to the budget guard from VG-004 — caps need history to be set sensibly.
acceptance_criteria: `vigil cost <planRoot>` prints total spend with breakdowns by plan, phase and model
`--since` and `--until` filter by run timestamp
`--json` emits the aggregate in the VG-013 envelope
Cache-read and cache-write token counts are reported separately from input and output tokens
Per-gate cost attribution is derived from events between gate boundaries and shown with --by-gate
Runs with malformed or missing cost.json are skipped with a warning rather than aborting the aggregation
Aggregating a 500-run synthetic corpus completes in under 2 seconds

features.title: Per-plan resume and resume-from-failed-gate
features.description: Complete the resume story. Apply recorded session ids per plan rather than only to the first, add `--resume-run <runId>` to continue a previous run from the first incomplete plan, and add `--resume-gate` to restart within a plan at the failing gate using recorded gate state. Resume decisions are shown in the cockpit and recorded as events.
features.rationale: Discovery marks session resume as partial: session ids are recorded and --resume is plumbed, but only a single id is applied to the first plan, with no per-plan resume UX. For multi-phase deployment work where phase one takes an hour, restarting from scratch after a phase-three failure is the dominant cost of a failed run.
source_pain_points: Session resume: session ids are recorded and --resume is plumbed, but only a single id is applied to the first plan — no per-plan resume UX
acceptance_criteria: session.json maps every plan id to its SDK session id and each plan resumes with its own id
`vigil run --resume-run <runId>` continues from the first plan without a terminal verdict, reusing prior gate records
`--resume-gate` restarts a failed plan at the failing gate rather than the plan start
Resumed runs write into a new run directory that records a parentRunId link to the original
The cockpit and --plain output state which plans were skipped as already-passed and which session ids were resumed
A resume attempt against a run whose plan files changed since the original is refused unless --force, detected via plan content hash
An e2e scenario fails a 3-plan fixture at plan 2, resumes, and asserts plan 1 is not re-executed

user_stories.as_a: operator whose 3-phase run failed at phase 3
user_stories.i_want: to resume from the failure
user_stories.so_that: I do not pay for and wait through two hours of already-validated work

user_stories.i_want: resumed runs linked to their parent run
user_stories.so_that: the full history of an attempt remains reconstructable

features.title: Evidence reconciliation on re-run
features.description: When a plan is re-run via the `r` key or a resume, reconcile evidence from the prior attempt instead of ignoring it. Stale artifacts are detected by hash and mtime against the prior GateRecord, and the operator chooses per policy whether to archive, delete or keep them. Gates whose evidence is unchanged since a prior FAIL are flagged so a re-claimed PASS over identical bytes is treated with suspicion.
features.rationale: Discovery notes that `r` re-runs the failed plan but state and evidence from the prior attempt are not reconciled. This is a live correctness hole in the trust model: an agent can fail a gate, and on re-run the pre-existing artifact from the failed attempt satisfies the existence check.
source_pain_points: Re-run after failure: `r` re-runs the failed plan but state/evidence from the prior attempt is not reconciled
acceptance_criteria: On re-run, each Capture target present from a prior attempt is hashed and compared against the prior GateRecord
config.reRunEvidence supports archive, delete and keep, defaulting to archive into evidence/.vigil-archive/<runId>/
A gate that PASSes on re-run with an evidence hash identical to a prior FAIL emits a distinct suspicious-evidence warning event and is surfaced in the report
Archived evidence is recoverable and its location is recorded in the gate record
The evidence overlay shows whether each artifact is new, unchanged or archived this attempt
A test fails a gate, re-runs with a stale artifact in place, and asserts the suspicious-evidence warning fires

user_stories.i_want: stale evidence from the failed attempt handled explicitly
user_stories.so_that: the retry cannot pass on artifacts the previous failure left behind

features.title: Run comparison and evidence diffing
features.description: A `vigil diff <runA> <runB>` command comparing two runs on gate verdicts, evidence hashes and content, cost, turn counts, tool-call sequences and rail hits. Output highlights verdict flips, evidence that changed between runs, and cost deltas, in table or JSON form.
features.rationale: Discovery lists run comparison and evidence diffing between runs as an opportunity. With hashes recorded by VG-003, comparison becomes cheap and directly serves the auditor persona asking what changed between a failing and a passing run.
acceptance_criteria: `vigil diff <runA> <runB>` reports per-gate verdict changes including gates present in only one run
Evidence differences are reported by hash, with a textual diff shown for text artifacts under a configurable size limit
Cost, turn count and tool-call count deltas are reported per plan
Rail hits present in one run and absent in the other are highlighted
`--json` emits the comparison in the VG-013 envelope
Runs of different plan sets are compared on their intersection with non-overlapping plans listed explicitly
Diffing two 10k-event runs completes in under 3 seconds

user_stories.i_want: to diff a passing run against a failing one
user_stories.so_that: I can see exactly which evidence and which tool calls differed

user_stories.i_want: hash-level evidence comparison between runs
user_stories.so_that: I can prove whether a re-validation actually re-produced its artifacts

features.title: Shareable run summary export
features.description: Export a single self-contained HTML or Markdown summary of a run: gate table with verdicts and evidence hashes, cost breakdown, rail hits, timeline of tool calls, and links to the artifacts on disk. acceptance_criteria: `vigil export <runDir> --format html|md` writes a single self-contained file

features.title: Pluggable plan adapters
features.description: Extract plan parsing behind an adapter interface so formats beyond the built-in XML-ish blocks can be gated. Ship the existing parser as the default adapter, add a simple Markdown-checklist adapter, and allow user-supplied adapters resolved from config by module path. Adapters produce the existing PlanModel, so the runner, evidence checker and reporter are unchanged.
features.rationale: Discovery notes Vigil is opinionated on one plan format and arbitrary markdown plans are not understood. Every team adopting the Claude Agent SDK already has validation checklists in some other shape; requiring a rewrite into a bespoke XML-ish format is a hard adoption barrier for the secondary audiences.
source_pain_points: Opinionated on one plan format (create-validation-plan XML-ish blocks) — arbitrary markdown plans are not understood
acceptance_criteria: A PlanAdapter interface defines detect(), parse() and contract() and is documented in docs/
The existing XML-ish parser is refactored into the default adapter with all parser.test.ts assertions passing unchanged
A Markdown-checklist adapter parses '- [ ] task' lists with Capture and Pass annotations into a valid PlanModel
config.planAdapter accepts a built-in name or a module path resolved relative to the config file
Adapter selection can be automatic via detect() when multiple adapters are registered, with ties reported as an error
A user-supplied adapter in the test suite gates a non-XML plan end to end without core source changes
An adapter returning a malformed PlanModel is rejected with a schema error naming the adapter

user_stories.i_want: to gate our existing markdown checklists

features.title: User-supplied rail and hook modules with lint mode
features.description: Allow rails, hooks and probe types to be supplied as user modules resolved from config, with a `vigil rails lint` command that validates patterns, detects unanchored or catastrophically backtracking regexes, reports overlapping rails, and dry-runs the full rail set against a corpus of recorded tool calls from previous runs to estimate false-positive rate.
features.rationale: Discovery lists user-supplied hooks/rails as modules, custom probe types, and rail dry-run/lint mode as opportunities. Since rails are the only gate on execution in the default mode, an authoring workflow that surfaces a bad pattern before a live run is a safety feature, not just ergonomics.
acceptance_criteria: config.railModules and config.probeModules resolve user modules relative to the config file and validate their exports against a schema
`vigil rails lint` reports invalid regexes, rails matching the empty string, and rails made unreachable by an earlier deny
Catastrophic backtracking risk is detected by evaluating each pattern against adversarial input under a timeout
`vigil rails lint --against <runDir>` replays recorded tool calls from that run through the rail set and reports which would have been denied or warned
Lint exits non-zero on any error-level finding so it can run in CI
A custom probe type supplied as a module emits probe RunEvents indistinguishable from built-in probes
Module loading failures produce a named error and refuse to start the run rather than silently running with fewer rails

user_stories.so_that: I can measure false positives before a rail blocks real work

features.title: npm publication and release automation
features.description: Publish Vigil to npm with an automated release pipeline: semantic versioning, a generated changelog, provenance attestation, a build-and-publish workflow triggered by tags, and a smoke test that installs the published tarball on a clean runner and executes a fixture plan.

source_pain_points: No license file, no CONTRIBUTING, no published npm package — install is npm link from a Desktop checkout
No CI configuration, no release automation, no changelog
acceptance_criteria: `npm i -g vigil` installs a working binary on a clean machine and `vigil --version` succeeds
A tag-triggered workflow builds, tests and publishes with npm provenance enabled
CHANGELOG.md is generated from conventional commits and updated on every release
The published package contains only bin/ and dist/ as declared in package.json files, verified by inspecting the packed tarball in CI
A post-publish smoke job installs the published version on a clean runner and runs the fixture plan in --plain --json mode
Publishing is blocked unless CI is green on the tagged commit
README install instructions reference the npm package rather than a Desktop checkout

features.title: Scrollable transcript and diagnostics search
features.description: Make the cockpit panes navigable: scrollback in the agent transcript and tools panes with keyboard paging and jump-to-latest, incremental search within the diagnostics pane with match highlighting and next/previous navigation, and a jump-to-gate shortcut that scrolls the transcript to where a verdict was emitted.

Combined with the constraint that content is heavily truncated below 110 columns, operators currently cannot review anything that scrolled past — undermining the live-observability promise during long runs.
source_pain_points: TUI requires a TTY; below ~110 columns the layout stacks and content is heavily truncated
Long autonomous runs are opaque — no live view of tool calls
acceptance_criteria: The transcript and tools panes support page up/down and home/end navigation with a visible scroll position indicator

A jump-to-gate shortcut scrolls the transcript to the point a selected gate verdict was emitted
Scrollback is bounded by a configurable maximum retained line count to cap memory on long runs
Existing keybindings are unchanged and the new bindings are listed in the help overlay
Snapshot tests from VG-010 cover scrolled and search-active states

features.title: Events consumer API and external dashboard streaming
features.description: A documented consumer API over the event stream — a library export for tailing events.jsonl with typed callbacks, plus optional webhook or WebSocket forwarding of RunEvents to an external dashboard or alerting system.
features.rationale: Listed as an opportunity in discovery, but deliberately deferred. Until the event schema is stabilised and versioned by VG-013 and the artifact layout is documented by VG-011, publishing a consumer API would lock in shapes that are still changing. Revisit after v1.0.
features.deferred_reason: Requires a stable, versioned event schema (VG-013) and documented artifact contracts (VG-011) to avoid locking in shapes that are still in flux. Premature publication would create backward-compatibility obligations during the phases that most need freedom to change the event vocabulary.
acceptance_criteria: Deferred beyond v1.0 — revisit once the RunEvent schema has been stable across two minor releases
Entry criteria: VG-013 schemaVersion unchanged across two releases and at least two external consumers requesting programmatic access

user_stories.i_want: to stream RunEvents into our dashboard
user_stories.so_that: agent runs appear alongside our other observability data

features.title: Remote control plane and multi-operator support
features.description: A server component allowing multiple operators to observe and control agent runs remotely, with authentication, per-user permissions and a shared run history.
features.rationale: Explicitly out of scope. Discovery states Vigil is a single-operator, single-machine tool with no multi-user, no server and no remote control plane, and this constraint is load-bearing: the disk-first, local-artifact trust model is what makes the audit guarantees simple and verifiable. Building a control plane would force authentication, transport security and a network trust boundary onto a product whose value is that everything is provable from local disk.
features.deferred_reason: Contradicts the core product constraint of a single-operator, single-machine tool and would compromise the disk-first trust model. `vigil tail` and the VG-013 JSON stream already serve the observe-from-elsewhere use case at a fraction of the cost.
acceptance_criteria: Not planned — explicitly out of scope for the v1.0 product
The remote-observation need is served by `vigil tail` and structured JSON output (VG-013) instead

user_stories.i_want: to watch an agent run from my own machine
user_stories.so_that: I can supervise without SSHing to the operator's box

dependency_graph.notes: Edges point from prerequisite to dependent. VG-001 and VG-003 are the two roots that unblock the widest downstream surface: VG-001 gates portability work, VG-003 gates every hash-dependent capability in Phases 4 and 5.

edges.reason: Scaffolding must emit neutral rails, not author-specific ones
Hardening is applied to the neutral rail set to avoid reworking author-specific patterns
Reports and de-duplication key on evidence hashes introduced by content assertions
Evidence reconciliation compares artifacts by hash
Run diffing compares evidence by hash
Aggregate cost reporting builds on run-level cost accumulation
Retention policy assumes artifacts are already redacted before long-term storage decisions
Exported summaries must pass through the redaction layer before sharing
The stubbed SDK harness targets the validated boundary interface
E2E suite needs a CI pipeline to run in
Snapshot tests need CI to be meaningful
Release automation requires green CI as a publish gate
JSON output contracts are asserted through the e2e harness
Resume scenarios are proven through the e2e harness
Adapter refactor is only safe with end-to-end coverage in place
Artifact schema documentation defines the JSON envelope
Adapter authors need a documented PlanModel contract
Publication requires a license and contributor documentation
A published package needs a first-run scaffold path
Resume relies on correct not_run and partial gate state
Export renders the corrected report model
Approval requests are emitted over the structured event channel
Aggregate output reuses the JSON envelope
Diff output reuses the JSON envelope
Reconciliation runs within the resume flow
Rail lint validates the hardened evaluation semantics
Module resolution infrastructure is shared between adapters and rails
Scroll and search states are verified through existing snapshot infrastructure

prioritization_summary.rationale: Must-haves are the features without which Vigil's stated promise is false or unusable: five Phase-1 items that make the tool installable by anyone and make the evidence and budget guarantees real, plus the Phase-2 durability trio that prevents mid-run crashes and silent regressions, plus structured output which is the prerequisite for the CI audience. Should-haves materially improve safety, correctness and reach but have viable manual workarounds. Could-haves are leverage on existing data or extensibility for audiences beyond the primary operator. Won't-haves are deferred pending schema stability (VG-025) or rejected as contradicting the single-machine, disk-first trust model (VG-026).

risks.risk: SDK coupling via unchecked casts against an exactly-pinned version
risks.mitigation: VG-006 replaces casts with validated schemas and widens the version range behind contract tests

risks.risk: Environment-specific defaults make the tool unusable by anyone but the author
risks.mitigation: VG-001 neutralises defaults into portable rails plus an example profile; VG-002 scaffolds per-machine config

risks.risk: Secrets captured verbatim into permanently retained run artifacts
risks.mitigation: VG-005 redacts at the single RunStore write chokepoint; VG-015 bounds retention

risks.risk: Rails are the only execution gate in default mode yet are bypassable via shell indirection
risks.mitigation: VG-009 normalises commands before matching and adds a strict mode; VG-022 adds lint and dry-run against recorded calls

risks.risk: Evidence check passes on wrong or truncated content, falsifying the product's core differentiator
risks.mitigation: VG-003 adds content assertions and hash recording; VG-018 prevents stale-artifact passes on re-run

risks.risk: Bus factor of one with no CI, so regressions surface only at runtime on production-adjacent machines
risks.mitigation: VG-007 and VG-008 establish automated gates; VG-011 and VG-023 lower the barrier to additional contributors

risks.risk: Synchronous appendFileSync per event throttles very chatty runs, worsened by added redaction and hashing work
risks.mitigation: Benchmark budgets in VG-005 and VG-003 acceptance criteria; revisit buffered or async writes in the RunStore if thresholds are breached

risks.risk: Scope creep toward a multi-user server erodes the disk-first trust model that makes audits simple
risks.mitigation: VG-026 is explicitly marked out of scope; remote observation is served by tail and VG-013 JSON streaming

sequencing_rationale: Phase 1 comes first because portability and honest guarantees are prerequisites for every other investment paying off — hardening a tool nobody else can install, or testing an evidence check that accepts wrong content, optimises the wrong thing. Phase 2 follows because Phases 3 to 5 all add surface area to the SDK boundary and the runner, and doing so without schema validation, CI and end-to-end coverage compounds the existing bus-factor risk. Phase 3 opens the secondary audiences (CI and SSH operators) once the core is trustworthy and tested. Phase 4 harvests the run corpus, which only becomes valuable after hashes exist (VG-003) and the schema is stable (VG-013). Phase 5 opens the product to contributors and publishes it, deliberately last so the extension points being frozen are ones that have survived four phases of change.
